summary: Extends SDP with two bandwidth modifiers that state how much bandwidth is allowed for RTCP packets in an RTP session. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RTP sessions carry two kinds of traffic: the media itself, and a control protocol called RTCP that reports on quality and timing. By default RTCP is allowed 5% of the session bandwidth. This RFC adds two lines to the session description so an application can set that share itself, separately for the senders and for the receivers.

questions: what are sdp rs and rr modifiers
how much bandwidth does rtcp use
how to turn off rtcp receiver reports
subtitle: Two SDP modifiers, RS and RR, that set how much bandwidth RTCP may use for senders and for receivers.

tldr.problem: RTCP normally gets 5% of the bandwidth in an RTP session, which is wrong for applications whose data rate adapts downwards and for applications that need to send extra RTCP information.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds two SDP bandwidth modifiers, b=RS for the RTCP bandwidth of active data senders and b=RR for that of the other participants, and defines their defaults, their precedence and how the two are split between senders and receivers.
tldr.outcome: A session description can now state the RTCP budget directly, which lets an application keep the RTCP share low when its data rate drops and lets it raise the RTCP share when it needs to send extra control information.

today:
RFC 3556 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the document that defines the RS and RR bandwidth modifiers for SDP.

The memo records that it was in conflict with the original SDP specification in RFC 2327, which prescribed integer kilobits per second for every bandwidth modifier, and that the fix was to give these two modifiers units of bits per second because the desired RTCP setting may be below 1 kb/s. The SDP specification was being modified at the time to allow that change in semantics.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) includes a control protocol, RTCP, which provides synchronisation information from data senders and feedback information from data receivers. Normally the bandwidth allocated to RTCP in an RTP session is 5% of the session bandwidth.

For some applications it is right to specify the RTCP bandwidth independently of the session bandwidth. A rate-adaptive application can set an RTCP bandwidth consistent with the typical data bandwidth it expects, which is usually lower than the maximum the session description advertises, and that keeps the RTCP bandwidth under 5% of the data bandwidth once the rate has adapted downwards. Other applications send data at very low rates but need to pass extra RTCP information, such as APP packets, and those need an RTCP bandwidth higher than 5% of the data bandwidth.

The RTP specification also allows a profile to split the RTCP bandwidth into two parameters, one for participants that are active data senders and one for those that are not. Two parameters make it possible to turn RTCP reception reports off for a session by setting the bandwidth for non-data-senders to zero, while keeping the bandwidth for data senders non-zero so that sender reports can still be sent for inter-media synchronisation. The document notes that turning off reception reports is not recommended, because the RTP specification needs them for reception quality feedback and congestion control, but it may be appropriate for systems on unidirectional links, or for sessions that do not need feedback on reception quality or receiver liveness and have other means of avoiding congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: An RTP session carries media in one direction and control reports in the other. The control reports normally get 5% of the bandwidth. This RFC lets the application write that share into the session description instead, so it can match the share to what the session is really doing.

sections.title: The RS and RR Bandwidth Modifiers
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol has an optional bandwidth attribute with the syntax b=<modifier>:<bandwidth-value>, where the modifier is a single alphanumeric word and the default unit of the value is kilobits per second. A typical use is the modifier AS, for Application Specific Maximum, which gives the total bandwidth for a single media stream from one source.

This memo adds two more modifiers: b=RS:<bandwidth-value> for the RTCP bandwidth allocated to active data senders, and b=RR:<bandwidth-value> for the RTCP bandwidth allocated to the other participants in the session, that is the receivers. What the modifiers do in practice depends on the algorithm used to calculate the RTCP reporting interval, and different RTP profiles may specify different algorithms.

For the RTP A/V Profile, which uses the default RTCP interval algorithm from the RTP specification, at least RS/(RS+RR) of the RTCP bandwidth is dedicated to active data senders. If the proportion of senders among the participants is less than or equal to RS/(RS+RR), each sender gets RS divided by the number of senders. When the proportion of senders is greater, the senders get their proportion of the sum of the two parameters, which means that a sender and a non-sender each get the same allocation. It is therefore not possible to constrain the data senders to use less RTCP bandwidth than is allowed for non-senders.

Three special cases follow from that rule. If RR is zero, the proportion of participants that are senders can never be greater than RS/(RS+RR), so non-senders never get any RTCP bandwidth whatever the number of senders. Setting RS to zero does not mean that data senders are not allowed to send RTCP packets; it only means that they are treated the same as non-senders. And if RS and RR are both zero, it would be unwise to attempt the calculation of the fraction RS/(RS+RR).
sections.plainLanguage: The session description now has two new lines for RTCP bandwidth. RS is the share for the participants that are sending media, and RR is the share for the ones that are only receiving. The document then works out how that total is divided when the numbers of senders and receivers do not match the values.

sections.title: Default Values
sections.content:
If either or both of the RS and RR specifiers are omitted, their default values come from the RTP profile in use for the session. For the Audio/Video Profile, RFC 3551, the defaults follow the recommendations of the RTP specification. The total RTCP bandwidth is 5% of the session bandwidth. If one of the two RTCP bandwidth specifiers is omitted, its value is 5% minus the value of the other one, but not less than zero. If both are omitted, the sender and receiver RTCP bandwidths are 1.25% and 3.75% of the session bandwidth respectively.

At least RS/(RS+RR) of the RTCP bandwidth is dedicated to active data senders, and when the proportion of senders is greater than RS/(RS+RR) of the participants, the senders get their proportion of the sum of these two parameters.

The memo does not impose limits on the values that may be specified with the RS and RR modifiers, other than that they must be non-negative, although the RTP specification and the relevant RTP profile may specify limits.
sections.plainLanguage: Leave the new lines out and you get the usual figures: 5% of the session bandwidth for RTCP in total, split into 1.25% for senders and 3.75% for receivers. If you write only one of the two, the other one takes whatever is left of the 5%, but never less than zero.

sections.title: Precedence Between Specifiers
sections.content:
An SDP description consists of a session-level part, holding details that apply to the whole session and to all media streams, and zero or more media-level parts, each holding details that apply to a single media stream. Bandwidth specifiers may be present at the session level to give the total bandwidth shared by all media, or in the media sections to give the bandwidth allocated to each medium, or both. The same is true of the two RTCP bandwidth modifiers.

Because the RTCP bandwidth is a fraction of the session bandwidth when it is not set explicitly, the session bandwidth and the RTCP bandwidth specifiers interact. The document sets out the precedence, with the first entry having the highest:

  1. An explicit RR or RS specifier at media level.
  2. An explicit RR or RS specifier at session level.
  3. A default based on the session bandwidth specifier at media level.
  4. A default based on the session bandwidth specifier at session level.

One consequence of that order is that setting the RR bandwidth to zero at session level turns off RTCP transmission for non-data-senders in all media.
sections.plainLanguage: A session description can carry bandwidth figures in two places: once for the whole session, and once for each media stream. The document lists which one wins, from the most specific to the least. The practical effect is that a session-level RR of zero switches off control reports from receivers across every media stream.

sections.title: Example Session Description
sections.content:
The memo gives a complete example: an SDP description for a seminar, with an audio medium and a video medium. The audio medium sets b=AS:64 together with b=RS:800 and b=RR:2400, and the video medium sets b=AS:256 with the same two RTCP values.

In the audio medium the explicit RTCP bandwidths are equal to the defaults, so they could be left out. For the video medium the RTCP bandwidths are set as though the data bandwidth were 64 kb/s, even though the maximum data bandwidth is given as 256 kb/s. That is based on the assumption that the video data bandwidth will automatically adapt to a lower value as network conditions change.
sections.plainLanguage: The example is a seminar with an audio stream and a video stream. The video stream advertises a maximum of 256 kb/s but sets its RTCP budget to what it would be for a data rate of 64 kb/s, because the rate is expected to drop when the network gets busy.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 2327 requires a new bandwidth modifier to be registered with IANA by reference to a standards-track RFC that specifies the semantics of the modifier precisely, indicates when it should be used, and explains why the existing registered bandwidth specifiers do not suffice. This document is written to satisfy those requirements.

Two new bandwidth modifier names have been registered in the bwtype table of the Session Description Protocol Parameters registry: RS and RR.
sections.plainLanguage: The two modifier names, RS and RR, are now recorded in the registry of SDP parameters, so other specifications can refer to them by name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo defines bandwidth modifier keywords as an extension to SDP, so the security considerations listed in the SDP specification apply to session descriptions carrying these modifiers as they do to any others.

It also warns that the bandwidth value supplied with one of the modifiers could be unreasonably large and cause the application to send RTCP packets at an excessive rate, resulting in a denial of service. That is similar to the risk of an unreasonable bandwidth being specified for the media data, though encoders generally have a limited bandwidth range. Applications should apply validity checks to all parameters received in an SDP description, particularly one that is not authenticated. The memo cannot specify limits itself, because they depend on the RTP profile and the application.
sections.plainLanguage: A session description can ask for an absurdly large RTCP budget, and an application that simply obeys it would flood the network with control reports. The advice is to check every value that arrives in a session description, especially one that has not been authenticated.

items.label: Application Specific Maximum
items.desc: The total bandwidth for a single media stream from one source.

items.label: RTCP bandwidth for senders
items.desc: The RTCP bandwidth allocated to active data senders, in bits per second.

items.label: RTCP bandwidth for receivers
items.desc: The RTCP bandwidth allocated to the other participants in the RTP session, in bits per second.

items.title: 1. Media level, explicit
items.text: An explicit RR or RS specifier at media level has the highest precedence.

items.title: 2. Session level, explicit
items.text: An explicit RR or RS specifier at session level comes next.

items.title: 3. Media level, default
items.text: A default based on the session bandwidth specifier at media level comes next.

items.title: 4. Session level, default
items.text: A default based on the session bandwidth specifier at session level has the lowest precedence.
